An important consideration for the retrofits is the type of HVAC system present in a particular household. Figure 9 shows that most single-family and mobile homes have ducted cooling systems with either traditional AC systems or heat pumps. Additionally, most multi-family dwelling units have similar configuration, with less than 25% of these having any type of shared HVAC system (for either heating or cooling). Most importantly, more than 90% of HVAC systems in PBC are individual systems. It is possible that repetition factors and economies of scale could allow for faster and less expensive retrofits for these individual systems, even in multi-family buildings. Furthermore, central AC systems can be upgraded to the highest efficiency HVAC systems much more directly as compared to households without ducts. Figure 9: Relative distribution of HVAC system configuration disaggregated by building type Another important characteristic when targeting homes for retrofits is the age of the building itself. Figure 10 shows the age distribution of households in PBC disaggregated by building type. The data show that mobile home and multi-family households are in general older than single-family households. It is important to note that in 1974, Florida enacted a law that required all local governments to adopt and enforce one of four model codes10. In 2002, the Florida Building Code was developed, which supersedes all local building codes and requires a single minimum standard building code which must be enforced by local governments10. Therefore, newer residential buildings can be assumed to have higher efficiency appliances and better building envelope characteristics (e.g., insulation and weather sealing) compared to buildings built before then. Additionally, building of certain ages may have other barriers to retrofitting include asbestos or lead paint that may increase the cost of the upgrade.
